newsitem.title: UK: IOD SAYS UK FISCAL RULES MUST TAKE ACCOUNT OF PFI.
newsitem.headline: IOD SAYS UK FISCAL RULES MUST TAKE ACCOUNT OF PFI.

text.p: The Institute of Directors (IoD) on Monday called on Britain's new Labour government to tighten fiscal rules to ensure that restraints on public spending took account of the Private Finance Initiative (PFI) scheme.

Stephen Davies, the IoD's economic research executive, said new rules for fiscal policy, announced by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown in his July 2 budget, left open the potential for a flood of "publicly sponsored" capital spending.
This included spending under the PFI plus conventionally financed public investment.

Such a flood of investment could severely stretch the construction industry and could also "fatally" undermine public expenditure control in the early years of the next century, the IOD said. The Private Finance Initiative was introduced by the former Conservative government as a way of relieving short-term pressure on the public purse by getting private sector companies to fund major projects such as building hospitals, roads and prisons. These would then be leased back by the government in future.
Brown has pledged to be prudent in running public finances and to abide by the "golden rule" of borrowing only to finance investment.
Davies said Brown's fiscal rules were flawed because they took no account of PFI spending in calculating the public debt to national income ratio.
"They provide no defence at all against the threat that the build-up of commitments under the PFI will overwhelm future public expenditure plans."

Accusing the government of conspicuously failing to define what it mean by "prudent" levels for the debt/income ratio, Davies urged it to develop a "PFI-adjusted public debt/national income ratio" as a new fiscal indicator.
